nameStory: The "spiderwort" name comes from the stringy, spider-web-like sap that oozes out when you break a stem or leaf. This clear, mucilaginous juice stretches into thin threads, just like a spider's silk! The "Ohio" part simply refers to where this species was first scientifically described, though it actually grows far beyond Ohio's borders.
description: Ohio spiderwort is a clump-forming perennial wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with long, grass-like leaves. Its most striking feature is its three-petaled flowers that bloom in shades of blue, purple, or occasionally pink, each lasting just one day. The plant forms dense colonies through underground stems, creating patches of these cheerful flowers in prairies and open woodlands. Its sturdy stems and narrow leaves give it an almost iris-like appearance when not in bloom.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Three rounded petals (never more, never less) in blue, purple, or pink with bright yellow stamens in the center. Each flower opens in the morning and closes by afternoon, becoming a jellylike blob.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves that fold lengthwise down the middle like a book. They feel smooth and slightly waxy, and emerge directly from the base and along the stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps 1-3 feet tall that spread into colonies. Stems are sturdy and jointed, like bamboo, with a swollen node at each joint that you can feel with your fingers.

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Break a leaf or stem and clear, stringy sap oozes out that stretches like spider silk between your fingers. This mucilaginous juice is unique and unmistakable.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, three-chambered capsules develop after flowering, eventually splitting open to release dark, wrinkled seeds that look like tiny raisins.

habitat: Look for Ohio spiderwort in sunny to partially shaded areas with moist, well-drained soil - prairies, meadows, roadsides, and open woodlands are prime spots. It thrives in disturbed areas and can often be found along railroad tracks and field edges. In New England, it's most common in the southern portions where it may be native or naturalized from cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as grass-like tufts, with flower buds forming by late spring. The distinctive jointed stems become apparent as the plant grows taller.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, with fresh three-petaled flowers opening each morning. The stringy sap is most noticeable during active growth.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules ripen, eventually splitting to release seeds. Leaves begin to yellow and die back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground growth visible. The plant survives underground through thick, fleshy roots and rhizomes.

funFact: Each spiderwort flower is essentially a living clock - it opens with the morning sun and closes forever by mid-afternoon, turning into a gooey, translucent blob that looks nothing like the beautiful flower it was just hours before!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Virginia spiderwort, but Ohio spiderwort typically has hairless or nearly hairless sepals (the green parts behind the petals), while Virginia spiderwort has distinctly hairy sepals. Remember: Ohio = hairless, Virginia = hairy sepals.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Ohio spiderwort is actually the most widespread spiderwort in North America, found from Maine to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas. Many garden center "spiderworts" are actually hybrids between this species and Virginia spiderwort, making wild identification sometimes tricky in areas where both species occur.
compareHints: Ohio spiderwort differs from Virginia spiderwort mainly in its hairless sepals and slightly more robust growth habit. Both species can hybridize where they meet, creating plants with intermediate characteristics. Unlike the tropical Purple Heart (also a Tradescantia), Ohio spiderwort dies back completely in winter and has much more temporary flowers that last only one day.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia spiderwort is the most common spiderwort in New England and has the classic blue-purple flowers and smooth leaves.

Compared to Virginia spiderwort (the most common spiderwort in New England), longbract spiderwort has much longer bracts extending well beyond the flower clusters, while Ohio spiderwort has hairless leaves (longbract's are slightly hairy).
Unlike its native New England spiderwort cousins like Virginia spiderwort, Purple Heart has distinctly purple foliage year-round rather than green leaves.
Unlike our native Virginia spiderwort with its grass-like leaves and blue flowers, inchplant has broad, striped leaves and rarely flowers indoors.
